teaching.causalExplanation: Start with the table. The stops label the rows and the columns. Each cell says how far it is between the row's stop and the column's stop, along one direct path. A dash means there's no direct path. Read along the Trailhead row. Six kilometres to the Lake, nine to the Mill, and dashes for the Ridge and the Village. Notice that the same six appears again, in the Lake row, under Trailhead. A path is the same length both ways, so the table is symmetric, a mirror image across its diagonal. That means you only need half of it. Now draw. Vertices first, five dots. Then each filled cell in the top half becomes an edge, with its number as the weight. Trailhead to Lake six, Trailhead to Mill nine, Lake to Mill four, Lake to Ridge seven, Mill to Village nine, and Ridge to Village three. Six cells, six weighted edges. Maps work the same way. Here's the trail map itself. The paths curve around hills and creeks, with their lengths printed beside them. To make a network, each stop becomes a vertex, and each path between two stops becomes an edge, with its length as the weight. The curves disappear, because a network only keeps what's joined to what, and the numbers we write on it. The map's scale and compass directions don't come across either. Only the stops, the paths and their lengths. And look. It's exactly the same network we drew from the table. A table and a map are just two ways of storing the same information. Now use it. What's the shortest ride from the Trailhead to the Village? With a network this small, list the possible routes and add the weights. Trailhead, Lake, Ridge, Village is six plus seven plus three, sixteen kilometres. Trailhead, Mill, Village is nine plus nine, eighteen. And Trailhead, Lake, Mill, Village is six plus four plus nine, nineteen. So the shortest ride is Trailhead, Lake, Ridge, Village, sixteen kilometres, even though the route through the Mill has fewer stops. And if you ride at twelve kilometres an hour, sixteen divided by twelve is one and a third hours, which is one hour twenty minutes. With bigger networks, listing every route gets out of hand, and there's a systematic method for that later in the strand.

Trailhead, Lake, Ridge, Village is six plus seven plus three, sixteen kilometres. Trailhead, Mill, Village is nine plus nine, eighteen. And Trailhead, Lake, Mill, Village is six plus four plus nine, nineteen. So the shortest ride is Trailhead, Lake, Ridge, Village, sixteen kilometres, even though the route through the Mill has fewer stops. And if you ride at twelve kilometres an hour, sixteen divided by twelve is one and a third hours, which is one hour twenty minutes. With bigger networks, listing every route gets out of hand, and there's a systematic method for that later in the strand.

scenes.teachingReason: Now the arrows change the answers. Drive from the Car park to the Pool, following the arrows. Car park to School, three, School to the Hall, four, the Hall to the Pool, two. That's nine minutes. Now come home. There's no arrow from the Pool to the Car park, so you go Pool to School, five, School to the Hall, four, and the Hall to the Car park, six. That's fifteen minutes, for the same two places. That's the network telling you something useful. A driver who only looked at the street map might plan the trip home completely wrong. In a directed network, always check which way the arrows point before you add a single weight.
